newsitem.title: USA: Conrail ordered to hold key meeting.
newsitem.headline: Conrail ordered to hold key meeting.

text.p: A federal judge Tuesday ordered Conrail Inc to proceed with a Dec. 23 shareholder vote the railroad had said would be postponed if it appeared unlikely to approve a key plank in a proposed $8.5 billion merger with CSX Corp..
U.S. District Judge Donald Van Artsdalen said it would be unfair to shareholders for Conrail to convene a company meeting for the vote only if the firm was assured of winning.
"To me, the way that this election is proposed to be held is fundamentally unfair to those who may be opposed," Van Artsdalen said. "That, as far as I can see, makes practically a sham election."
The decision boosted Conrail's stock price on speculation CSX may have to raise its bid in order for Conrail to win shareholder approval.
Conrail expressed regret at the ruling, but said it had not decided whether to appeal. The company is free to convene another meeting later if it loses the shareholder vote next week.
The ruling also allows the meeting to be postponed if there is a material change in circumstances surrounding the deal, such as the emergence of a new bidder or higher bid from CSX.
Van Artsdalen was ruling on a request by Norfolk Southern Corp., which has made a rival, $10 billion cash bid for Conrail, to block Conrail from postponing next week's meeting.
Shareholders are to vote at the meeting on whether to waive a Pennsylvania state law effectively requiring CSX to pay all cash for Conrail. CSX has offered 40 percent cash and 60 percent stock.
Conrail had said in voting materials mailed to its shareholders that it would probably postpone the meeting if it could not round up enough votes.
Shareholders typically vote on corporate issues through proxies returned in advance of a meeting to the companies, although they may vote or change their vote at the meeting.
An influential shareholder advisory group last week recommended voting against the waiver, in view of the higher Norfolk Southern offer and possibilities the bidding war could continue.
Asked by Van Artsdalen in a hearing before the ruling whether Conrail intended to proceed with the meeting, Conrail attorney Tom Van Kirk said he was unable to say.

CSX attorney Paul Rowe said in the hearing that an unfavourable ruling would cast in a bad light Conrail's conduct in the merger process. "That would be viewed as putting the entire transaction under a cloud," he said.

After the ruling, Conrail general counsel Bruce Wilson said, "We regret that the court has seen fit to interfere with what unsually are normal and clearly disclosed corporate processes, especially where no decision has been made to postpone the Dec. 23 meeting."

Norfolk Southern attorney Steven Rothschild welcomed the ruling as a victory for shareholder rights. "What we have always wanted is for the Conrail stockholders to be given a right, without coercion, to express their view, whatever that view is," Rothschild said.

Norfolk Southern said in a statement: "Shareholders will have a meaningful vote on December 23 and by voting against the 'opt out' proposal will be a step closer to having the opportunity to consider Norfolk Southern's superior offer -- an offer worth about $16 per share or $1.5 billion more than CSX's coercive front-end loaded, two-tiered deal for Conrail."
Conrail stock traded up $1.75 at $98.125 in late New York Stock Exchange trading. Takeover stock specialists said CSX may have to raise its bid early to win the vote.

But they said the impact of the ruling was limited because Conrail can simply call another vote if it loses next week's, or it can bypass a waiver vote altogether by asking stockholders to vote on the entire merger itself on a later occasion.
